findings.quote: at this time we are still waiting for the ACCG audit to be signed off so that we can review the work which they have performed.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council - Audit Findings Report - 2024-25 - Audit Committee
findings.headline: £11m overstatement found in land and buildings valuations
findings.detail: Auditor testing identified an £11m overstatement in land and buildings valuations during asset revaluation. Although the auditor assessed this as not material to the overall accounts, management declined to adjust the accounts.
findings.matters: A £11m overstatement in the Council's largest asset class (total L&B £1,196m) indicates control or valuation methodology weaknesses affecting reliability of balance sheet asset values.
findings.figures: £11m overstatement; Land and Buildings total £1,196m
findings.quote: The difference we identified of an overstatement £11m is not material and so management have not adjusted the accounts for this matter.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council - Audit Findings Report - 2024-25 - Audit Committee
findings.headline: PFI liabilities restated upwards by £3.8m
findings.detail: PFI liabilities were restated to reflect indexation of unitary payments since scheme inception. This resulted in a £3.8m increase to the opening PFI liability at 1 April 2024, reflecting retrospective adjustment for inflation-linked obligations.
findings.matters: A £3.8m upward restatement of committed long-term PFI payment obligations indicates either prior accounting omission or material increase in the Council's debt obligations.
findings.figures: £3.8m increase to opening liability
findings.quote: the PFI liabilities are required to be restated on transition to reflect the indexation of unitary payments since the start of the schemes. This has resulted in a £3.8m increase of the opening liability at 1 April 2024.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council - Audit Findings Report - 2024-25 - Audit Committee
findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting adds £1.8m of new liabilities
findings.detail: Implementation of IFRS 16 from 1 April 2024 resulted in £1.8m of additional lease liabilities and Right of Use Assets being recognised on the balance sheet. These were previously off-balance sheet as operating leases.
findings.matters: Off-balance sheet obligations brought onto the balance sheet increase the Council's stated debt burden and liabilities, materially affecting net financial position.
findings.figures: £1.8m of additional lease liabilities
findings.quote: The implementation of IFRS 16 has resulted in £1.8m of additional lease liabilities and Right of Use Assets recognised on the balance sheet in respect of former operating leases.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council - Audit Findings Report - 2024-25 - Audit Committee
findings.headline: Six significant weaknesses in value-for-money arrangements identified
findings.detail: The auditor identified six significant weaknesses in the Council's arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness. The auditor is not satisfied that the Council has made proper VFM arrangements. Detailed findings are in the separate Auditor's Annual Report presented at the November 2025 Audit Committee meeting.
findings.matters: A council lacking proper arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness presents material risk to lenders regarding financial management capability and operational control.
findings.figures: Six significant weaknesses
findings.quote: We identified six significant weaknesses in the Council's arrangements and so are not satisfied that the Council has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council - Audit Findings Report - 2024-25 - Audit Committee
findings.headline: Police investigations prevent audit certification
findings.detail: The external auditor cannot formally close the audit or issue an audit certificate until outcomes of two ongoing police investigations into the Council are known. The auditor states this does not have a material effect on the financial statements for 2024-25 but it is blocking statutory sign-off.
findings.matters: Unresolved police investigations into a council are a governance red flag and prevent auditors from completing their statutory duties, creating uncertainty around control environment and account closure.
findings.figures: Two ongoing police investigations
findings.quote: However, we cannot formally conclude the audit and issue an audit certificate in accordance with the requirements of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014 and the Code of Audit Practice until the outcomes of the two ongoing police investigations relating to the Council are known.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 Final For Publication
findings.headline: Property Services improvement plan stalled: Strategic Asset Management Plan not adopted; corporate landlord model incomplete
findings.detail: The auditor notes 'some key building blocks of the original improvement plan are yet to be implemented'. Specifically, 'The Council has not yet adopted the revised Strategic Asset Management Plan and there is slippage in fully rolling out the corporate landlord model. This creates strategic, operational and financial risk.' The auditor updated the 2023-24 key recommendation on this.
findings.matters: Property represents a material asset and cost base. Unimplemented asset strategies and slow corporate landlord adoption suggest hidden costs (maintenance, inefficient space) and deferred savings that will not land as planned.
findings.figures: Strategic Asset Management Plan not yet adopted; corporate landlord model rollout incomplete
findings.quote: The Council has not yet adopted the revised Strategic Asset Management Plan and there is slippage in fully rolling out the corporate landlord model. This creates strategic, operational and financial risk.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 Final For Publication
findings.headline: Internal audit opinion downgraded to Limited Assurance; high-priority recommendations overdue by 6+ months
findings.detail: The Chief Audit Executive issued a Limited Assurance Internal Audit Opinion for 2024-25, 'indicating that there are significant control weaknesses that present a high risk to the control environment'. There has been a 'significant increase in outstanding Directorate internal audit recommendations' with 'a significant number of high priority and strategic recommendations overdue for longer than six months'. The auditor escalated this from an improvement recommendation to a key recommendation.
findings.matters: Internal control failures create unpriced risk for a lender. If the council cannot execute its own improvement plans or embed audit recommendations, it is unlikely to hit its stated savings or revenue targets.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance opinion issued; significant recommendations overdue 6+ months
findings.quote: Internal audit provided a Limited Assurance Internal Audit Opinion for 2024/25, indicating that there are significant control weaknesses that present a high risk to the control environment.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 Final For Publication
findings.headline: Homelessness Service ballooned from £13.1m overspend (2024-25) to £15.9m forecast overspend (2025-26)
findings.detail: The Homelessness Service overspent by £13.1m in 2024-25 and is now forecast to overspend by £15.9m in 2025-26—a 22% increase in just one year. The auditor notes 'Demand within the Homelessness Service also continues to create significant financial pressure and risk'. This also reflects an open 2023-24 key recommendation on cost management.
findings.matters: Homelessness is an open-ended statutory duty. Escalating overspends in this area show the council is losing control of a major cost driver, which could force disproportionate cuts elsewhere or further reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: Homelessness overspend: £13.1m (2024-25); forecast £15.9m (2025-26)
findings.quote: The service overspent by £13.1m in 2024/25 and pressures continue into 2025/26 with a forecast overspend of £15.9m as at Month Five.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 Final For Publication
findings.headline: Children's and Adult Social Care overspends persistent: £15.5m and £3.3m in 2024-25, both forecast to overspend again in 2025-26
findings.detail: Children's Social Care overspent by £15.5m and Adult Social Care by £3.3m in 2024-25. The auditor notes both services 'have significant forecast overspends as at Month Five 2025/26'. This mirrors a key recommendation from 2023-24 that remains 'open'—the council has failed to bring these pressures under control.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether cost growth is temporary or structural. Two years of consecutive overspends in high-cost services, with no improvement forecast, suggest demand or efficiency issues the council cannot manage within budget.
findings.figures: Children's Social Care: £15.5m overspend 2024-25; Adult Social Care: £3.3m overspend 2024-25
findings.quote: Children's Social Care overspent by £15.5m in 2024/25 and Adult Social Care by £3.3m. While the Council is taking action to try to mitigate budget pressures, these services both have significant forecast overspends as at Month Five 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 Final For Publication
findings.headline: Savings pipeline slippage: £13.9m (19%) of £68m target undelivered as at March 2025
findings.detail: The council proposed an £85.6m three-year savings pipeline in 2023-24. By end of 2024-25, £13.9m had not been delivered—a 19% miss. For 2025-26, this £13.9m slippage is now rolled into a £41.7m savings target, and Q1 monitoring shows £13.9m of that at risk (red/amber RAG rated).
findings.matters: Savings plans that slip year-on-year signal weak programme management and eroding confidence in the council's ability to rebalance. A lender sees this as proof that stated deficit-closing plans are overstated.
findings.figures: £13.9m undelivered from £68m 2023-24/2024-25 target; £41.7m 2025-26 target; £13.9m at risk
findings.quote: there have been challenges to savings delivery, with £13.9m undelivered (19%) as at March 2025 when measured against the £68.0m total target for 2023/24 and 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 Final For Publication
findings.headline: Cumulative budget deficits forecast at £26.7m (2026-27) rising to £60.3m (2027-28)
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy now forecasts a £26.7m gap in 2026-27, growing to £60.3m by 2027-28. The council acknowledges these gaps 'must' be bridged by a Transformation Programme that is 'essential' to financial sustainability, but delivery to date has been patchy.
findings.matters: A lender is pricing medium-term creditworthiness. A £60m structural deficit in 18 months, with no certain savings plan to close it, is a material risk to refinancing capacity.
findings.figures: Budget deficit £26.7m in 2026/27; £60.3m in 2027/28
findings.quote: significant cumulative budget deficits were forecast of £26.7m in 2026/27, rising to £60.3m in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 Final For Publication
findings.headline: Quarter One 2025-26 reveals £29.6m forecast overspend despite 'balanced' budget approval
findings.detail: Even after building £52.3m of growth into the 2025-26 budget to address service pressures, budget monitoring at Q1 identified cost and demand pressures exceeding planning assumptions by £29.6m. The auditor explicitly states this threatens the planned reserve rebuild and could force 'difficult choices in 2026/27'.
findings.matters: A lender is concerned about budget execution risk and the council's ability to control spending. A £29.6m miss in just three months signals structural problems, not one-off issues.
findings.figures: £29.6m forecast overspend at Month Five 2025-26; £52.3m growth built into budget approval
findings.quote: budget monitoring at Quarter One 2025/26 identifies that cost and demand pressures are exceeding planning assumptions, with forecast budget pressures of £29.6m identified.

findings.paper_title: Liverpool City Council Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 Final For Publication
findings.headline: General Fund balance depleted to £16.8m from £36.8m after £20.0m overspend in 2024-25
findings.detail: The council set a balanced budget but experienced a net £20.0m revenue overspend, mainly in social care and homelessness. This forced a 54% drawdown of reserves from the recommended prudent level. The council now holds 'very low levels of reserves which impacts on its ability to respond to unforeseen financial pressures'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has financial headroom to absorb service shocks; at £16.8m reserves on a £1bn+ budget, it has essentially none.
findings.figures: General Fund balance reduced from £36.8m to £16.8m; net revenue overspend £20.0m
findings.quote: The net overspend was funded from the General Fund balance, reducing it from its recommended level of £36.8m to £16.8m at March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - Treasury Update Quarter 3
findings.headline: Investment returns fell from 4.25% to 4.05% following Bank of England rate cuts
findings.detail: Following BoE base rate cuts on 8 May and 7 August 2025, the average return on liquid investments has declined. Returns in the first 8 months of the year averaged 4.25%, but the latest average return has dropped to 4.05% as the lower rate environment affects cash deposits and money market holdings.
findings.matters: Lower investment returns reduce non-service revenue and the finance base available to support council expenditure, affecting overall financial stability
findings.figures: Average return 4.25% (first 8 months) to 4.05% (latest)
findings.quote: The average return on investments in the first 8 months of the year was 4.25%. Following the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) bank rate cut on 8 May and subsequently 7th August, the return from liquid investments has dropped, with the latest average being 4.05%

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - Treasury Update Quarter 3
findings.headline: Investment holdings fell £32.7m in Q3 to £83.7m from £116.4m in August
findings.detail: Total investments declined significantly in the quarter, with Money Market Funds down £23.2m and Bank Deposits down £10m. The council maintains a minimum investment balance of approximately £50m by year end as part of its cash management strategy.
findings.matters: Investment balance levels and trends affect the council's liquidity position and available reserves to fund operations and weather unexpected pressures
findings.quote: Total Investments 69.5 116.4 83.7 14.2 (32.7)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - Treasury Update Quarter 3
findings.headline: £115m of new borrowing arranged in September-November 2025 to fund capital program
findings.detail: The council arranged substantial new borrowing in Q3 comprising £70m from other local authorities at rates of 4.45%-4.50%, £5m from banks at 4.15%, and £40m from PWLB at rates of 4.62%-4.63%. This reflects ongoing capital financing to support the anticipated rise in capital financing requirements for the year.
findings.matters: The scale and cost of capital borrowing is a key indicator for lenders assessing the council's capital program funding strategy and debt servicing capacity
findings.figures: £115m total: £70m from LAs (4.45%-4.50%), £5m from banks (4.15%), £40m from PWLB (4.62%-4.63%)
findings.quote: The following borrowing was arranged during Sept - Nov 2025: LA £5m 4.45%, LA £10m 4.50%, B/S £5m 4.15%, LA £10m 4.45%, PWLB £20m 4.63%, PWLB £20m 4.62%

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee 061125 - Treasury Mid Year Report Final
findings.headline: Capital programme reprofiled with in-year borrowing need cut from £83m to £48m; reason not stated
findings.detail: The Treasury Management Strategy projected an £83m in-year borrowing requirement to finance the capital programme. The capital programme has since been reprofiled, reducing the projected borrowing need to £48m — a 42% reduction. The report provides no explanation for this material change, leaving unclear whether it reflects project deferrals or financial constraints.
findings.matters: A large reduction in planned capital financing needs explanation: it may signal either routine resequencing or reduced spending ambition driven by balance sheet pressure. The absence of explanation creates uncertainty about capital delivery plans.
findings.figures: Original in-year capital borrowing requirement £83m; revised projection £48m; reduction of £35m or 42%
findings.quote: The capital programme has been subject to reprofiling since approved at the March budget meeting, meaning the in-year requirement to finance the capital programme is currently projected to be £48m.

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee 061125 - Treasury Mid Year Report Final
findings.headline: Internal borrowing capacity is under pressure from forecast General Fund overspends and DSG deficits
findings.detail: The council has historically managed capital investment by using internal reserves and positive cashflows rather than external borrowing. However, the report explicitly states that forecast overspends in the General Fund and Dedicated Schools Grant are now constraining this approach. If these overspends remain unmitigated, balance sheet resources will be depleted, forcing the council to increase external borrowing beyond planned levels.
findings.matters: When reserves are consumed by operational shortfalls, a council's financial flexibility erodes and debt service costs rise. A lender needs to know whether the balance sheet can support both operating deficits and capital investment without destabilizing debt levels.
findings.figures: Actual borrowing at mid-year £949m; total long-term obligations £1,008.9m at 30/9/25; operational boundary for borrowing 2025/26 set at £1,098m
findings.quote: the council's ability to sustain previous levels of internal borrowing is increasingly under pressure due to forecast General Fund overspends and DSG deficits. If projected overspends remain unmitigated it will deplete the balance sheet resources used to support internal borrowing and has the potential to push up borrowing levels.

findings.paper_title: Income and Debt Recovery Assurance Audit Committee Nov 2025 (002)
findings.headline: £13.6m in bad debt written off in 2025/26, indicating collection limits
findings.detail: The council wrote off £6.891m in council tax, £4.183m in sundry debt, £2.056m in Adult Social Care, and £0.569m in housing benefit overpayments. Write-offs are approved only after recovery options are exhausted, covering statute-barred debts, deceased residents with no estate, and residents who cannot be traced.
findings.matters: Write-offs reduce net recoverable revenue and show the council reaches practical limits in collecting various debts, affecting true cash-generative capacity.
findings.figures: Council Tax: £6.891m; Sundry Debt: £4.183m; ASC: £2.056m; Housing Benefit OP: £0.569m
findings.quote: Before approval is given to write off a debt all recovery options must be exhausted

findings.paper_title: Income and Debt Recovery Assurance Audit Committee Nov 2025 (002)
findings.headline: Court process delays blocking resolution of £3.86m in Adult Social Care debts
findings.detail: The top 30 Adult Social Care debts total £3.86m. The council identifies Court of Protection applications and probate proceedings as the primary barrier to further recovery. These are judicial delays outside the council's control that prevent cash collection despite active recovery efforts.
findings.matters: These debts cannot be recovered on schedule due to procedural constraints in the court system, directly reducing the council's actual cash flow from recoverable receivables.
findings.figures: Top 30 ASC debt balance: £3.86m; originally £3.22m in October 2023, now includes new debts as older ones are cleared
findings.quote: A key barrier to resolution pertains to ongoing delays in court processes, particularly in progressing Court of Protection applications and probate matters. These legal and procedural delays continue to impact recovery timelines, despite sustained efforts to move cases forward.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Children's Services remained inadequate at May 2023 Ofsted inspection; improvement continuing but not yet validated
findings.detail: Ofsted judged Children's Services inadequate overall in May 2023, with inadequate ratings in three key areas. The council has invested in improvement including new leadership and a transformation programme. Recent Ofsted monitoring visits (most recent March 2025) show progress in some areas (disabled children, missing children) but note gaps remain, particularly in multi-agency response to child exploitation and governance fragmentation.
findings.matters: Inadequate children's services is a reputational risk and can lead to higher intervention or council takeover. More immediately, improvement programmes are costly, and if they do not land before the next full inspection, the council faces further deterioration and potential for statutory direction.
findings.figures: Ofsted ILACS inspection May 2023 (inadequate); monitoring visits March 2025; in-house children's home inspection April 2025 (judged good)
findings.quote: In 2023 the Council's Children and Young People's directorate was subject of an Ofsted Inspection of Local Authority Children's Services (ILACS). The report was published in May 2023 and judged the council to be inadequate in three key areas and requires improvement in a fourth key area.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Risk management not fully embedded across the council
findings.detail: The statement notes: 'Evidence suggests that risk management is not fully embedded across the Council and further work needs to be done to ensure a robust risk management culture and process exists and is operating effectively.' A risk management software solution is still in final testing. This is an area flagged for improvement in the 2025/26 work plan.
findings.matters: Weak risk management means the council may not identify emerging financial or operational problems early enough to manage them. Combined with low reserves and audit control weaknesses, this increases the risk of financial deterioration going unnoticed.
findings.figures: Risk management software in final testing; e-learning mandatory from 2023
findings.quote: Evidence suggests that risk management is not fully embedded across the Council and further work needs to be done to ensure a robust risk management culture and process exists and is operating effectively.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: NHS restructuring creates risk of cost-shifting to council for vulnerable children and adults
findings.detail: Cheshire and Merseyside ICB is in financial turnaround and required to make 50% cuts to administrative costs. The ICB's budget constraints are focused on services not directly provided by NHS, including Continuing Health Care, Section 117 aftercare, SEND, and Better Care Fund services. The council states: 'The key risk is that the NHS will seek to reduce its expenditure in the expectation that the Council will meet costs of services to vulnerable adults and children to prevent harm.'
findings.matters: This is an external cost pressure. If the NHS withdraws funding for services the council is legally required to provide, the council's already-strained Adult Social Care and Children's Services budgets will face additional unfunded growth.
findings.figures: Cheshire and Merseyside ICB required to make 50% reduction in administrative costs; weekly oversight and monitoring being undertaken
findings.quote: The key risk is that the NHS will seek to reduce its expenditure in the expectation that the Council will meet costs of services to vulnerable adults and children to prevent harm.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Demand-led overspends in Adult Social Care, Children's Services, and Housing with no named mitigations in place
findings.detail: Adult Social Care and Health, Children and Young People's Services, and Neighbourhoods and Housing all overspent in 2024/25. From July 2024, budgetary controls were implemented to try to contain overspends at directorate level, but the outturn report in July 2025 shows these services still overran. No mitigations are named in the statement.
findings.matters: Demand-led services (social care, housing) are difficult to control because the demand is determined by the size and characteristics of the population, not by the council's budget. Persistent overspends suggest the budget envelope is set below what the council must spend to meet legal duties.
findings.figures: Overspends in Adult Social Care and Health, Children and Young People's Services, Neighbourhoods and Housing reported in outturn July 2025
findings.quote: This outturn report shows the significant impact on the financial health of the council as a result of the financial challenges in demand-led services, with overspends in Adult Social Care and Health, Children and Young Peoples Services and Neighbourhoods and Housing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Internal Audit gives Limited Assurance with high risk to control environment
findings.detail: The Director of Internal Audit's 2024/25 opinion is Limited Assurance rather than Reasonable Assurance. The opinion explicitly flags a high risk to the control environment. This reflects that governance, risk and control frameworks are mainly operating as intended but significant gaps remain.
findings.matters: Limited Assurance is a low bar—it means the auditor cannot give confidence that controls are working reliably. A high-risk control environment means there is material risk of fraud, error, or noncompliance.
findings.figures: 2024/25 audit opinion
findings.quote: The Director of Internal Audit provides limited assurance that the Council's governance, risk and control framework is mainly operating as intended with a high risk to the control environment.
